messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mere Tuilagi is a 63-year-old Fijian-American woman who works as a project manager for a regional construction firm in Phoenix, Arizona. She has been married for thirty-four years and describes her husband as her closest confidant, though she acknowledges that even he cannot fully reach her now. She was referred for psychological assessment following a conversation with her primary care physician, who noted her persistent reluctance to attend follow-up appointments and her visible distress during routine examinations.

Approximately eighteen months ago, Mere was admitted to hospital in acute respiratory failure secondary to a rapidly progressing bacterial pneumonia that had been initially misdiagnosed as a seasonal chest infection. What began as a week of fatigue and shortness of breath ended with Mere losing consciousness at home and waking in an intensive care unit with a central line running into her neck, an oxygen mask pressing against her face, and her wrists loosely restrained to prevent her from pulling at the drip lines she could feel but not see. She later learned she had been unconscious for four days. What she remembered was more fragmented: the cold pressure of the cannula entering the back of her hand, the particular angle at which her neck was turned against a pillow she could not adjust, the sound of an alarm she could not interpret, and a sustained sensation of drowning from the inside.

In the weeks after her discharge, Mere returned to work earlier than her doctors recommended, telling herself that structure would help. For a time, it did. But her office environment, where project timelines are reviewed in long team meetings, became unexpectedly difficult to navigate. When colleagues raised topics about hospital delays in construction supply chains — a recurring industry problem — or when conversations drifted toward illness, injury, or medical costs, Mere found herself abruptly unable to follow the thread of the discussion. She described it not as distraction but as a sudden and total absence, as though the room continued without her. What frightened her most in those moments was that she could not find words for what was happening to her. The experience of the ICU had not organized itself into a story she could tell; it existed instead as sensation and position, as the specific weight of her body immobilized and the cold tracking of fluid into her vein. When the memory returned, it did not arrive as a recollection. It arrived as the thing itself — the smell of antiseptic, the restraint at her wrists, the drowning — and her body assumed the posture of those four days without her choosing it.

She had come to believe that her body had fundamentally failed her, and that it might do so again without warning. She no longer trusted the signals it sent. A tight chest after climbing stairs was not fatigue; it was the beginning of something catastrophic. She had quietly stopped attending her scheduled follow-up appointments, finding reasons to reschedule, and when her husband accompanied her to a routine blood draw, she became rigid the moment the phlebotomist uncapped the needle. She asked to leave before the draw was completed. She did not explain to her husband why, because she could not explain it to herself in language.

At work, she had grown short-tempered in ways that surprised people who had known her for years. An unexpected hand on her shoulder from a colleague had once prompted a sharp, audible gasp and a response that she later described as mortifying. She had difficulty sustaining concentration across the long planning documents that were central to her role, and a project she had been managing for two years had slipped in ways her supervisor had begun to notice.

Mere had come to feel that the woman who had managed complex builds and raised two children and cooked elaborate Sunday meals had been replaced by someone she did not recognize and could not trust. She had told her husband, in a rare moment of disclosure, that she felt her life as she had known it was simply gone. What finally brought her to seek help was not any single incident but the accumulation of distance — from her work, from her husband, from the body she lived in. She arrived at the intake appointment hoping, above all, to be believed.
